title: Yathā vṛkṣasya: the flowering tree and the sword over the pit
theme: Two images: good deeds spread like the scent of a tree in flower; wrongdoing is a sword’s edge over a pit, to be avoided with great care.

words.context: Sāyaṇa: «सम्यग्विकसितपुष्पोपेतस्य» — with its flowers fully open
Sāyaṇa: «सत्कीर्तिः सुगन्धसमाना» — good repute, like a fragrance
Sāyaṇa: «कर्ते कूपादावगाधे कस्मिंश्चिद्गर्तविशेषे» — over a well or other deep pit
Sāyaṇa: «यौमि यौमि पुनः पुनः पादमसिधारया मिश्रयामीत्यर्थः» — if I press my foot on the edge again and again
Sāyaṇa reads «विह्वदिष्यामि» and glosses «विह्वलितो विवशो भविष्यामि» — I shall be shaken, helpless

words.meaning: from the deathless / from untruth (see ambiguities)
words.role: what one guards oneself from or for
words.context: Anonymous: «अमृतान्मोक्षप्राप्तिहेतोः» — for the sake of reaching release; Sāyaṇa: «पुरुषोऽनृतात्पापादात्मानं जुगुप्सेद्धिङ्मां» — from untruth, sin
Sāyaṇa: «धिङ्मां लोकद्वयभ्रांशहेतुमिति निन्दित्वा पापान्निवारेत्» — blaming himself, he should turn back from sin

sandhi.type: t before a voiced consonant; aḥ before a voiced consonant; i before a dissimilar vowel
sandhi.rule: dūrāt → dūrād before g; gandhaḥ → gandho before v; vāti + evam → vāty evam.
yathā + asidhārām → yathāsidhārām; the print marks the merged a with avagraha (यथाऽसि).

sandhi.type: e before a; m before a vowel
sandhi.rule: After -e an initial a is elided, marked by avagraha (karte ’vahitām; P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति)); avahitām avakrāme.

sandhi.type: i + i; i before a dissimilar vowel; m before a vowel; t before a vowel
sandhi.rule: patiṣyāmi + iti → patiṣyāmīti; iti + evam → ity evam; evam amṛtād ātmānam.

morphology.note: A Vedic first-person middle form of √yu, ‘join’. Sāyaṇa: the text has ha where y would be expected, which is why some read yuve yuve («हकारो व्यत्ययेन यकारस्थाने पठितः। अत एव केचिद्युवे युव इति पठन्ति»); Bhāskara reads ‘whether here or there I join [the edge or the pit]’ («इह वा असिधारां यौमि इह वा कर्तं यौम्य्»).

The base and both witnesses read amṛtāt. Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara explain the word as anṛtāt, ‘from untruth’ (Bhāskara: «अस्यापि वर्णान्यत्वं छान्दसम्», a Vedic change of letter); the anonymous commentator keeps amṛtāt, ‘for the sake of the deathless’.

translation.literal: As the fragrance of a tree in full flower wafts from afar, so the fragrance of a meritorious deed wafts from afar. As one might walk along a sword’s edge laid across a pit, [thinking] “if I press, if I press [my foot] I shall be disabled, or I shall fall into the pit” — so should one guard oneself from the deathless [untruth].
translation.readable: Good deeds, like a flowering tree, send their fragrance far. But wrongdoing is like walking a sword laid over a pit: press down and the blade cuts, step off and you fall. With that same care one should hold oneself back from untruth.

syntax: Two yathā … evam comparisons. The first is a simple statement. The second sets a scene (yathā asidhārām karte avahitām avakrāme), quotes the walker’s thought (yad yuve … patiṣyāmi, closed by iti), and draws the rule with evam and the optative jugupseta.

ambiguities.note: As printed, ‘from the deathless’ reads oddly. The anonymous commentator takes it as ‘for the sake of the deathless, release’, steadying the mind and shrinking from sin; Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara read anṛtāt, ‘from untruth’, and Bhāskara explains the letter as a Vedic variation.

The commentators struggle with these words: Sāyaṇa reads ha as ‘I’ and huve for yuve; Bhāskara ‘whether here or there I join’; the anonymous commentator ‘if I go, if I go’. All agree on the sense: whichever way one steps, harm follows.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose, one printed line of 72 syllables; no metre is claimed.

beginner: Two pictures. First, a tree in full bloom sends its scent a long way; so do good deeds — the commentators say their good name spreads, even to heaven. Second, imagine walking along the edge of a sword laid across a deep pit. The walker thinks: if I press down, the blade will cut my foot and I will stagger; if I step aside, I will fall into the pit. Either way there is harm. So, the text says, one should hold oneself back. From what is unclear in the printed word: Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara read “from untruth”, while the anonymous commentator reads it as guarding oneself for the sake of release. The commentators explain: done in the open, wrongdoing brings blame here; done in secret, it brings suffering hereafter. The record reports these readings.
analogy: Like a tightrope over a canyon: the rope cuts if you lean on it, the canyon waits if you step off; the only safety is not to start across.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: As the scent of a flowering tree wafts from afar, so does that of a meritorious deed. As one who would walk along a sword’s edge laid over a pit thinks “if I press I shall be disabled, or I shall fall into the pit”, so should one guard oneself — from amṛta as printed, from untruth as the commentators read.

commentary.q: What is the point of the two images?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: the passage praises prescribed meritorious action as a means to knowledge and blames forbidden action as an obstacle to it — «अथ विहितानुष्ठानरूपं पुण्यं ज्ञानसाधनतया प्रशंसति। निषिद्धचरणं ज्ञानप्रतिबन्धकतया निन्दति». The fragrance is good repute, which reaches even heaven («सत्कीर्तिः सुगन्धसमाना दूराद्वाति मनुष्यलोकात्स्वर्गे गच्छति»).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa describes a performer who walks a blade over a pit to entertain a king, and reasons as he does: «यद्यहं पापं प्रकटं कुर्यां तदानीमिह लोके निन्दितो भविष्यामि तत्परिहारायाप्रकटं कुर्यां तदाऽपि नरके पतिष्यामीति» — open wrongdoing brings blame here, hidden wrongdoing brings hell. The anonymous commentator draws the same lesson and concludes ‘so I will do no wrong, in public or in secret’ («तस्माद्बही रहसि च न पापं करिष्य इत्युपरम्यताम्»).

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: All three witnesses read अमृतात्. The anonymous commentator keeps it: one seeking release should steady the mind for the sake of the deathless and shrink from sin («अमृतान्मोक्षप्राप्तिहेतोरात्मानमन्तःकरणं स्थिरीकृत्य पापाज्जुगुप्सेत्»). Sāyaṇa glosses «पुरुषोऽनृतात्पापादात्मानं जुगुप्सेद्धिङ्मां», and Bhāskara explains the letter as a Vedic change, concluding «सर्वथा अनृताद् आत्मानं परिहर्तुं यतेतेति». The base is kept; both readings are given.

schools.disagreement: The commentaries available are ritual and Vedic; none takes a position on which the Vedānta schools named here divide. No Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available here).

parallels.note: The Kaṭha calls the path to the self ‘the sharp edge of a razor, hard to cross’; here the blade over the pit is the image for avoiding wrongdoing.

contemporary.text: The first image says good conduct travels on its own, like scent; the second says that with wrongdoing there is no safe way across — exposed or hidden, it costs. Both are about how actions outrun the moment they are done in. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Why might good deeds be compared to a smell rather than to something you can see?
reflect.deeper: Does “guard oneself from the deathless” make sense as printed, or is the commentators’ “from untruth” needed? What would each imply?
reflect.practice: Think of one thing you would not want to do even if no one ever found out, and notice why.

flags.note: amṛtāt is kept as printed; Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara read anṛtāt, ‘from untruth’, the anonymous commentator ‘for the sake of the deathless’.
